title: 16 Celebs, One Underground Bunker, Zero Loyalty: Kunal Kemmu's 'Alliance' Is Prime Video's Most Ruthless Game Yet
excerpt: It premieres June 26 in 240 countries at once — the first time Prime Video has gone global with an Indian unscripted format. The catch? The whole thing is built on a lie.
body:
The man rushes onto the floor, breathless. "The names of the alliances have arrived." And then Kunal Kemmu, all sharp suit and sharper grin, turns to camera and drops the line that reframes the entire show: "Duniya mein aane ke liye tumhe doctor ke haath lagte hain, aur jaane ke liye chaar kandhe. You didn't arrive alone and you won't leave alone either — because this world runs on alliances. But none of that is going to happen here."

https://youtube.com/watch?v=XvCJ9g-XJgo

That is the bait, and the betrayal, of Alliance — Prime Video's new Hindi-language unscripted series that drops June 26, and the streamer's boldest reality swing in years. Sixteen celebrities walk in as eight duos, each pair bound by something real: blood, marriage, friendship, a career built side by side. Then the format spends 42 episodes pulling those bonds apart, one whispered betrayal at a time.

**"The truth is — from day one, their alliances will break." — Kunal Kemmu, in the trailer

It is a deliciously cynical premise, and the casting leans straight into the drama."**

"The difference is, we've lied to the contestants. They think that because the show is called Alliance, they'll form alliances. The truth is — from day one, their alliances will break." — Kunal Kemmu, in the trailer

It is a deliciously cynical premise, and the casting leans straight into the drama. There's Ravi Kishan entering alongside his Gen-Z influencer daughter Riva Kishan — a father-daughter act that the game will surely try to fracture. Reality-TV veterans Kushal Tandon and Arslan Goni bring the simmering bad-boy energy. Zaid Darbar and Daisy Shah, Mini Mathur and her real-life husband Nikhil Chinapa (yes, the MTV power couple is playing), Niti Taylor and Ruhee Dosani, Vanshaj Singh and Dolly Javed, gamer Payal Dhare with Sabby Suri, and Delbar Arya with Armaan Khera round out the roster. It's a deliberate cocktail of television faces, digital stars, and one or two people who clearly came to win.

The setting is half the seduction. Forget the sun-drenched villas of most reality shows — Alliance is staged inside a sleek, high-tech underground secret facility, a bunker where luxury meets paranoia. Every room is designed to be a stage for confrontation: marble and mood lighting on the surface, a pressure cooker underneath. The Allies face an explosive mix of physical challenges, knowledge games, secret missions, and out-and-out manipulation, all in pursuit of points to survive. Two eliminations a week, two wildcard entries to keep everyone off balance, and a fresh episode dropping every single day at noon.

That daily cadence is the part that should make rivals nervous. Alliance is the first international adaptation of Talpa Studios' acclaimed Dutch format — created by Big Brother mastermind John de Mol — produced here by Banijay Asia. And it arrives at a moment when the unscripted space is suddenly crowded: Lock Upp Season 2 lands on Netflix with Farah Khan and Riteish Deshmukh just a day later, and the next Bigg Boss looms on the horizon. For viewers, it's a glut. For the platforms, it's a war for the second-screen audience.

For Kemmu, it's a reinvention. The actor — long one of Bollywood's most underrated leading men and, lately, a confident director — steps into hosting for the first time, and the trailer suggests he's a natural: dry, watchful, faintly amused by the carnage he's presiding over. "It's not just about winning challenges," he said ahead of the launch. "It's about navigating relationships, making tough choices, and adapting when the game changes around you."

Here's where it gets interesting for the diaspora: Alliance isn't a domestic-only drop. It premieres simultaneously in India and across more than 240 countries and territories — a first for Prime Video with an Indian original of this kind. That means NRI viewers in the US, UK, Canada, Australia and the Gulf get the same noon-IST episode their cousins in Mumbai are watching, no VPN gymnastics required. For a generation of desis abroad who've turned group chats into live reality-TV war rooms, that synchronicity is the real prize.

Forty-two episodes. Six weeks. One bunker full of people who came in trusting each other and will leave doing anything but. The only honest thing about Alliance may be Kemmu's warning: inside this game, no bond is guaranteed, and no one is safe.
